title: Digital Multimeter Basics & CAT Ratings

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Bench with the company-issued DMM, test leads, probe tip covers and a test-lead holder. Matthew behind the bench, medium shot.
scenes.says: Job Mindset for your meter. The hazards: a meter that fails and explodes in your hand from a voltage spike, an arc from leads in the wrong jack, and a false dead reading from a weak battery. The controls are the right rating, an inspection before every use, and checking your setup every time. Pack spare batteries and the right fuses before you leave.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up of the meter dial; Matthew's finger moves across V~, V DC, ohms, continuity, amps, LoZ.
scenes.on_screen: LT1: AC voltage. Continuity and resistance on dead circuits only. No amps.
scenes.says: At LT1, you'll mostly use your meter for AC voltage, to verify absence of voltage. Resistance and continuity, the beep setting, are for de-energized circuits only. The amps settings aren't used at LT1. Clamp meters are safer, and you'll get those at LT2.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up of the jacks: black lead plugged into COM, red into V. Then the red lead moved to the A jack with a red X graphic.
scenes.on_screen: Black in COM. Red in V. Dial on V.
scenes.says: The jacks. Black lead in COM, always. Red lead in V for voltage, resistance and continuity. The A and milliamp jacks are for current. Here's why that matters. If the red lead is in an amps jack and you touch the probes across a voltage source, you create a near short through the meter. Even with good fuses, that can cause an arc flash in your hands.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Simple building graphic: utility meter and service entrance (CAT IV), lighting panel and branch circuits and hardwired fixtures (CAT III), plug-in lamp at a receptacle (CAT II). Matthew voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: CAT IV: service entrance | CAT III: panels, branch circuits, fixtures | CAT II: plug-in loads
scenes.says: CAT ratings. Electrical systems get spikes from lightning and switching, bigger near the service entrance, smaller downstream. CAT ratings show how big a spike a meter survives without failing in your hand. CAT IV is the service entrance and utility meter. CAT III is building wiring: lighting panels, branch circuits, hardwired fixtures. CAT II is plug-in loads.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up of CAT markings on the meter and on the leads; an independent lab mark on the case.
scenes.on_screen: At least CAT III 600 V. Lowest-rated part sets the rating.
scenes.says: Category and voltage go together. For building lighting circuits, use a meter and leads rated at least CAT III 600 volts. Higher category at the same voltage is better. And the system's only as good as its lowest-rated part. A CAT III 1000-volt meter with CAT II leads is a CAT II system. Look for an independent lab mark, too.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech inspects the meter case, display and battery indicator, runs the leads through his fingers, checks finger guards, snaps on shrouded tip covers, seats the plugs. Matthew voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Case - Display and battery - Leads - Probes and guards - Connectors - Fuses
scenes.says: Inspect before every use. Case: no cracks or signs of overheating. Display clear, no low-battery symbol. A weak battery can give false readings. Leads: no cuts or melted spots. If you see the colored inner layer, replace them. Probes: tips tight, finger guards intact, shrouded tip covers on. Plugs fully seated. Check fuses the maker's way, and replace only with the exact rated fuse.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up on Matthew holding the meter, display reading a few volts.
scenes.says: Reading the display. OL on voltage means over range. On resistance, it means open. Watch your units. And ghost voltage: a meter can show voltage on a disconnected wire running next to live ones. LoZ mode can make it collapse. But never assume a reading is just ghost voltage. Stop and get a qualified person to evaluate it.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Tech at a de-energized training panel, standing to the side, using a test-lead holder, fingers behind the guards. Matthew voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Fingers behind the guards. Stand to the side.
scenes.says: Good habits. When one point is a known neutral or ground, black lead on first and off last. Fingers behind the finger guards. Use a test-lead holder where you can, so one hand stays away from grounded metal. And stand to the side of panels and disconnects, not in front.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.on_screen: Now read the lesson and take the quiz
scenes.says: Right rating, inspected, black in COM, red in V, dial on V. Every time. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: No energized measurements needed; the amps-jack mistake is shown with the meter disconnected and a red X graphic only. The habits demo uses a de-energized training panel. CAT location graphic should be simple and generic. Meter and lead brands not visible; use the licensee's company-issued model if possible.
